description: Branched perennial herb, up to 1 m high, glabrous. Stem irregularly branched, terete or somewhat tetragonal, several from a thick rhizome. Leaves ovate in outline, deeply pinnately or sub-bipinnately 3-7-lobed, up to 10 cm long, petiolate; petiole up to 3.5 cm long; leaf segments simple or 3-partite, glabrous, linear or narrowly elliptic rather thick and coriaceous; apex acute to acuminate, indurate; margin entire, subrevolute. Capitula erect, broadly funnel-shaped or hemispheric, 1-2(-3) at the ends of terminal peduncles 3-4.5 x 0.7-0.9 cm at anthesis; peduncle glabrous, up to 16 cm long; receptacle glabrous or pubescent. Phyllaries differentiated in shape, size and colour. Outer phyllaries green, 4-8, linear, or narrowly elliptic, 4-14 mm long, sparsely pubescent at base; apex acute or obtuse, callose-thickened. Inner phyllaries greyish orange with scarious margin, c. 8, oblong, glabrous except the puberulous apex, 6-10 mm long. Ray florets yellow, 5-8; ovary aristate, neuter; rays narrowly elliptic-obovate with 13-20 dark brown striae, 1.5-3 cm long; apex entire or minutely 3-fid; tube glabrous or sparsely pubescent. Paleae thin, c. 7-10 cm long, linear, obtuse. Disc florets yellow; corolla 5-lobed, narrowly funnel-shaped above, glabrous. Achenes black or dark brown, linear-oblong, obcompressed, hispidulous or glabrescent with a few short bristles near the apex and margins, 6-7 x 1.2-1.6 mm; apex with a ring of short erect, irregularly-sized bristles, bi-aristate; aristae entire except for the few bristles at base and a single antrorsely or retrorsely set one at apex, c. 2 mm long.

description: Erect annual herb, 20-150(-250) cm high; stem tetragonal, glabrous or minutely setose-hispid especially in young plants, sometimes densely branched. Leaves opposite, rarely alternate towards apex, bipinnatisect, usually pubescent in lower parts, ovate in outline, up to 20 cm long, petiolate; segments membranous, ovate to deltoid or terminal one lanceolate, vein reticulation characteristic, ciliate; margin crenate-serrate, ciliate; petiole usually ebracteate, 1-6 cm long. Capitula erect, radiate, 4-7 x 4-6 mm at anthesis, up to 20 mm high in fruit (incl. achene aristae), in lax paniculate cymes; receptacle sparsely white-pubescent, globose, 3-4 mm in diameter; peduncle glabrous, rarely sparsely ciliate, striate-sulcate, up to 10 cm long. Outer phyllaries green, linear or lanceolate, 7-10, glabrous or ciliate at base, 3-striated, 3-5 x 0.5 mm at anthesis, slightly dilated towards apex, shorter than the inner phyllaries; apex acute. Inner phyllaries dark brown (after drying) with yellowish white scarious margins, ciliate at base, 7-8, linear, 3-6 x 1 mm at anthesis, margins ciliate near apex. Ray florets yellowish white, 3-5, neuter; ray lamina c. 5 x 1.5 mm; apex entire or 3-fid, with 5 orange striae, oblong; tube c. 1 mm long. Paleae membranous, pale brown, linear-lanceolate, c. 3-5 x 1 mm, up to 10 mm long in fruit, glabrous. Disc florets yellow, cylindric, not annularly thickened or constricted medially; corolla 5-lobed, c. 4 mm long; anthers brown, c. 1 mm long; style c. 3.5 mm long. Achenes black, linear-fusiform, tetragonal, glabrous or sparsely tuberculate-hispid towards apex, 7-18 x 1 mm; apex truncate with 4 (rarely 2 or 3) yellow, slightly divergent, retrorsely barbed aristae, 2-4 mm long.

description: The distribution of M. densa is more or less equivalent to the distribution of the entire genus. M. densa is most common in the western Cape and quite rare in the northern part, e. g. in Namaqualand. In the Little Karroo and eastwards M. densa is partly replaced by other quite closely related species, such as M. trivialis, M. massonii and M. aurea. From the eastern Cape and northwards M. densa, like other Cape elements, becomes a high-mountain species. North of the Drakensberg range M. densa is more scattered, with the extremity of its distribution in the western Soutspansberg at 23° S. It is the only species which extends far outside the Cape region.

description: Plants that more or less precisely match the type of the name S. erubescens range from the Cape peninsula (e.g. Table Mt. near Rosebank, Bolus 10740) east to Humansdorp, Port Elizabeth and Albany. Here for the first time forms with toothed rather than lobed leaf margins begin to appear. Head size may also increase slightly, reflected in up to 20 involucral bracts, up to 9 mm long (Port Elizabeth, near the Golf Course, Marriott PRE 20363). From about the Amatola Mts. eastwards through the Transkei to Natal and the Transvaal (and to tropical Africa ?) a recognizably different form appears to replace true S. erubescens: usually no basal rosette, stems decumbent, densely leafy in the lower half (with a strong tendency for the leaves to be pushed to one side of the stem) the inflorescence branches pedunculoid with a tendency towards a thyrsoid-racemose rather than a corymbose-paniculate arrangement of the heads. These plants can be referred to S. erubescens var. crepidifolius DC.

description: E. lateriflorus belongs to the most widely distributed South African species of the genus. It occurs mainly in karroo areas from southern S. W. The species is especially common in the Central Upper Karroo of the Roggeveld and Nieuweveld (mainly Galvinia and Sutherland Divisions), where it is sometimes the dominating shrub of large areas. description: One population, characterized by large total size and light lemon-coloured flowers (see below) grows on sand in the Olifants River Valley (Clanwilliam Division). It merges into stiffer and lower forms on sandy and clayey substrates. Forms near Strand and Gordon's Bay (Somerset West Division) grow on veritable sand dunes on the coast, and some forms grow on marine sand substrate near Piketberg, south of Worcester, near Bredasdorp, near 'Darling Bridge', in the Wolseley region, etc. all on sandy substrate. Other forms grow on clayey substrate, e.g. in the Breede River Valley (Worcester Division) and in the Malmesbury and Riviersonderend regions, where the vegetation is a mixed fynbos scrub/renosterbos rather than Cape fynbos.

description: A. baptisioides inhabits sourveld areas where grass cover is sparse while A. longifolium often occurs where grass cover is dense. Both occur in Ngongoni Veld, Highland Sourveld and Dohne Sourveld. The disjunction of A. baptisioides which occurs in the Transkei is a common anomaly in east coast plant taxa. Weimarck (1941) referred to the area as the Kaffraria Interval which he claimed results partly from the inability of the 'Cape element to penetrate xeromorphic biotypes of the Great Fish River Valley'. This explanation is unsatisfactory as the distributional gap occurs to the north of the valley. A plausible explanation is the discontinuity in sandstones for about 600 km in the Transkei (Van Wyk 1990). The southernmost outcrops of Natal Group sandstones occur at Port St. Johns and the northern exposures of the Cape Supergroup occur at Suurberg. The intervening landscape is Karoo Sequence interspersed with dolerite intrusions from which A. baptisioides and its allies are absent.

It is found more or less throughout the dry southern part of Namibia and extends eastwards as far as Upington and Vanwyksvlei in South Africa. description: Widely distributed over the southern part of South West Africa and the northern, western and southern Great Karoo below about 1300 m above sea level. Its northern limit is the dune-sea north of Lüderitz-Aus and from here the plants are scattered over a wide area across to Prieska and Douglas. In the southern part of South West Africa, this species occurs west of the high plateau, though not reaching the sea. In South Africa, however, it does not occur west of the Namaqua granites or the mountains of the Richtersveld. It is plentiful in Bushmanland and is found in the Tanqua and Montagu-Oudtshoorn Karoo, as well as the lower Great Karoo as far east as Prince Albert. It has not been found in the intervening escarpment and high plateau that stretches from Sutherland to De Aar and further.

description: Orbea lugardii has been surprisingly rarely collected and there were only a few records of it in southern African herbaria. However, a concerted effort to record it wherever it was encountered has revealed it to be widely distributed over much of southern Africa. This collecting has shown that it is of almost universal occurrence in Namibia, except in the winter-rainfall area south of Helmeringhausen, the arid Namib Desert along the coast, in the sands of the relatively moist Ovamboland and in the Caprivi. In Botswana it is mainly found in the west (probably more widely towards the south than the existing records show) and in the central parts of the Okavango Delta. In South Africa it is found in two areas. One is in the region from Upington and Kimberley northwards into the Kalahari and the other lies in the extreme northern corner of the country north of the Soutpansberg. From here there is only a single record and it may prove to be more widespread in this area. White & Sloane also mention its probable occurrence in Zimbabwe but this has not been confirmed by any records. It remains a possibility also that it might occur in southern Angola.

description: Tromotriche aperta has an essentially coastal distribution in the arid parts of south-western Namibia and the north-western Northern Cape, well within the winter-rainfall area. In Namibia it is known from the vicinity of the Aurus Mountains and the Obib Mountains, which lie to the west of Rosh Pinah. South of this there appears to be a gap in the distribution, and T. aperta begins to appear once more around Lekkersing. From here it continues sporadically southwards to Soebatsfontein and between Wallekraal and Garies. It is found a little further east around Eksteenfontein but this seems to be the only area where it ventures off the coastal plain and away from the low, coastal hills.

description: Stapelia gigantea is the most widely distributed species of Stapelia in a north-south direction. Plants have been collected in Zambia and Malawi and over a very wide area in Mozambique. In all these countries the collections are few and extremely widely dispersed. They are also recorded (Leach 1985) from Kenya and Tanzania but both these specimens are most likely to have been escapes from gardens and it seems that S. gigantea is not indigenous there. In Botswana it is found along the eastern side, from Nata southwards to near Lobatse. It is widespread in the lower-lying parts of Zimbabwe and in the north-eastern parts of South Africa. In KwaZulu-Natal, the southernmost records have been made near Stanger.

description: Larryleachia perlata appears to occur in two disjunct areas. The larger of these areas begins in the mountains west and east of Rosh Pinah in southern Namibia and continues southwards across the Orange River to Sendeling's Drift and around Kubus. Plants are also found eastwards to Vioolsdrift and near Goodhouse and as far as the dry valley of the Wyepoort River a little north of Steinkopf. The other, very much smaller area appears to be isolated from the main body of the distribution and lies in the Klinghardt Mountains in the coastal Namib Desert about 100 km south of Lüderitz.

description: No other protea is so widely distributed as P. gaguedi. It ranges from Kwa Zulu in South Africa, throughout central Africa to Eritrea in north-eastern Ethiopia. In South Africa its distribution range extends in a narrow tongue from the Soutpansberg in the northern Transvaal, southwards along the eastern Transvaal escarpment (where it is especially prominent along the Blyde Canyon) to Barberton, Swaziland and Utrecht in northern Natal, with the most southerly populations occurring in the Nsuze River Gorge west of Eshowe in Kwa Zulu. Isolated outliers also occur in the northern foothills of the Magaliesberg, near Rustenburg and Brits. Immediately beyond our borders, P. gaguedi is found in Rhodesia, the Okavango area of northern Botswana, as well as at a few localities in the Caprivi Strip, and in southwestern and central Angola.

description: R. barrosiana is known from approximately 26° 45' to 31° 31'S latitude and from 29° 30' to 32° 45' E longitude; from coastal situations only slightly above sea level to altitudes not exceeding 1000 m. It is probably present on the Mocambique plain, although we have seen no specimens from there. Records exist from the border of Mocambique and Natal (Kwa Zulu), southwards along the coast just into northernmost Transkei (Sea View). Furthest inland records are Eshowe and Noodsberg (both these localities verge on the inland limit of coastal Natal according to Ross 1972). Therefore this species has a much more restricted distributional and altitudinal range in the Flora area than has R. brownii. It must be regarded as a taxon with more tropical habitat requirements. The possibility that R. barrosiana might represent an introduction to southern Africa by way of a centre such as Durban was considered. Its presence in remote, undisturbed natural situations seems to negate this, however.

description: Leucadendron pondoense is strictly riverine with a very limited distribution range extending in a narrow band over a distance of about 40 km along the so-called Wild Coast of Pondoland. At present the southernmost record is from the Sikatsha River near the village of Cutweni, and the northernmost a confirmed sight record below the spectacular Nxa Xas Falls on the Mnyameni River. Possibly because of less severe flooding, the species is found mainly along the many short and relatively small streams and rivers originating in the area of the coastal scarp. It is particularly common within about 5 km from the coast along the lower reaches of the Cutweni, Mfihlelo, Mlambomkulu, Lupatana, Mkweni, Daza and Mkambati Rivers.

description: This widespread, variable species is distributed over much of central zone southern Africa, from the equator southwards, occurring chiefly in Uganda, Tanzania, Zaire, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, Angola, Rhodesia and South Africa. In South Africa, P. welwitschii has a rather disjunct distribution. It is sporadically dispersed over the western and southeastern Transvaal from Potgietersrust along the Waterberg to the Marico hills near Zeerust in the west; thence to the Magaliesberg and Witwatersrand, extending to Middelburg and the high eastern Transvaal escarpment at Belfast, Machadodorp and Lydenburg. Isolated populations also occur in Natal, between Umzinto on the south coast and Nkandhla in KwaZulu, ranging inland as far as Pietermaritzburg and Greytown.

Both species occur to the west of Pietermaritzburg, between Impendhle and Richmond. In this area, A. amatymbica occurs at lower elevations, while A. cordifolia is found at higher altitudes - the two species may be found in close proximity but their distribution areas do not appear to overlap.

description: The species is known from approximately 23° to 34°S latitude and from 18°30' to 32°50'E longitude. The western-most relatively recent record from the southern Cape is Esterhuysen 31393 (BOL) (coll. 17 Nov., 1965) from the south slopes of Riversonderend Mts near Lindeshof, Caledon area. In 1830, Ecklon collected the species from Table Mountain, Ecklon 867 (BOL!, K, MO) (alt. c. 1000 m). It has not been recollected from the Mountain (see note by Levyns 1950: 118). The (BOL) specimen carries slightly immature inflorescences and so has not been cited nor mapped. Its identity is not in doubt, for no other Rhynchospora species in southern Africa approaches such westerly limits (all others fall away before 29°E), according to present records. Dinter 1803 from South West Africa (cited by Podlech 1967) (M?) has not yet been examined. This seems to be the only record for the species from north-western localities within the Flora area. The distribution of R. brownii is interesting from its altitudinal range also. Relatively few sedges with a range from the Cameroons through tropical Africa and down the eastern part of the continent extend as far west as the Cape Peninsula. The fall away is generally between Port Elizabeth and Mossel Bay. The answer seems to be that at tropical latitudes, R. brownii is represented only at fairly high altitudes. It becomes frequent in coastal localities round about 27°S. Collectors along the Mocambique coast do not seem to have recorded it, but it is likely to be present on the Gorongoza massif. Other species that are represented both in tropical Africa and at the Cape have a more inland mountain distribution and are not found near sea level in Natal.

Plants with certain traits of ssp. biseriata have been found on the lower slopes of Blousteenberg facing False Bay in Caledon Div. (! 3590). It is also widespread, though somewhat less common, on the Great Karoo as far east as the Free State and the northern Eastern Cape near Maclear. Subsp. caespitosa is found in most suitably dry habitats in the Western Cape from southern Namaqualand to the Worcester-Robertson Karoo, the Ceres Karoo, Little Karoo and the Great Karoo as far east as Graaff-Reinet, Fort Beaufort and Grahamstown. Further east of this it becomes scarce, with only a few localities known in the Free State and the northern Eastern Cape.

description: Sutera levis is endemic to the Transvaal and neighbouring parts of Botswana; it appears to be commonest along the Magaliesberg and the Witwatersrand and on the Highveld as far south as the Vaal and east to Middelburg; there is one record from Waterval Boven but its presence there needs confirmation. Holub collected it near Zeerust at the end of the last century and there is another old collection from Schweizer-Reneke and one from the western extremity of the Waterberg. Apart from these, there are no collections west of Rustenburg except those from Botswana; Ootse in Botswana is about 65km NNW of Zeerust. From the Magaliesberg, it ranges over the Springbok Flats about as far north as the 23rd parallel.

description: This is primarily a plant of the south eastern Transvaal, from Mount Anderson, near Lydenburg, south almost to the Assegai River. With a clearer understanding of what is, and what is not, N. angustifolia, a review of some of the labels in herbaria is called for. It may be that the Maolangampisiberg or the Belelasberg form the southern boundary and that in Natal the place of N. angustifolia is taken by N. appendiculata. A recent collection, not yet seen in flower, from near Glencoe may be important. The position of related plants in Swaziland to the east and the Orange Free State to the west will need further study.

description: It appears to be endemic to the mountains of the eastern Cape, between Katberg, Cathcart and Stutterheim. On Katberg, we found it in straggling masses along a streamlet on the edge of the road through the forest, but beyond the summit of the pass it formed big clumps down a streamline; on Thomas Mountain it grew among rocks beside a stream in a deep narrow valley as well as among rocks on the moist face of a steep slope, partly sheltered by trees and bushes. On the Windvogelberg it is common on the S-facing slope near the summit beacon, among rocks and big tufts of Merxmuellera; here the plants were very bushy, not as lax as specimens from wetter sites, nor with such big leaves.

description: Quaqua mammillaris is the most widely distributed of all species of Quaqua and occurs over most of the western parts of the Karoo. It is found from the Klinghardt Mountains south of Lüderitz in Namibia southwards into Namaqualand and right across the drier parts of the Northern and Western Cape, mainly west of the escarpment, to as far east as near Rietbron in the Great Karoo and Oudtshoorn in the Little Karoo. It also occurs in the area around Warmbad in Namibia and Pofadder in Bushmanland of South Africa.

description: Quaqua multiflora is known to occur over a relatively wide area towards the eastern edge of the winter-rainfall region. It is known from a few places around Matjiesfontein, then roughly 200 km to the north at several localities north-east, south and south-east of Calvinia. Recently I located a further, quite substantial colony a little south of Leliefontein in the Kamiesberg, about 200 km to the north-west of Calvinia, and a few specimens were also found east of Springbok. This remarkably disjointed distribution is similar to that of Adromischus phillipsiae and, as in this species which has quite stringent requirements of habitat, this patchiness in the distribution appears to be real rather than a consequence of inadequate collecting.

description: The Q. parviflora-complex consists of several allopatric forms. They occur in the winter-rainfall area in Namaqualand from Clanwilliam northwards to west of Steinkopf around Anenous and Steenbok. Some of these forms occur eastwards as far as Loeriesfontein, Calvinia and parts of the Ceres Karoo. Many of them have, at some stage or other, been recognised as separate species. However, as carefully explained in Bruyns, this does not accurately reflect their relationships, nor are they easily and reliably separable from one another and consequently they continue to be recognised here as subspecies of a single species.

description: Subsp. dependens is quite common along the southern boundary of Namaqualand. It is mainly found in the area from Citrusdal to Klawer where the vegetation is transitional from fynbos to karroid scrub. Here it grows mostly on drier, stony lower slopes among shrubs. It has also been recorded further east in Botterkloof, where it grows with subsp. gracilis. Further populations are known near the mouth of the Olifants River in the sandveld, growing in deep red soils covered with spiny grasses and a wide variety of succulent shrubs.

description: Across southern Africa: In Namibia, it is known from four localities. Two are in the Tiras Mountains south-west of Helmeringhausen and the other two lie some 250 km to the south-east, at an altitude of over 2000 m in the Great Karas Mountains and around their base at about 1400 m near Grünau. In the Northern Cape it has been found widely from west of Kenhardt to Williston and near Middelpos, apparently avoiding the flat, pan-like parts of Bushmanland. Further east it is widespread from Fraserburg to Griquastad, Douglas and to Cradock as well as south to Aberdeen Road. There is a single collection from near Fauresmith in the Free State. This distribution is remarkably similar to that of Ceropegia filiformis and bears some similarity also to that of Piaranthus cornutus and Fockea sinuata.

description: Duvalia polita is the most widely distributed of all the ‘southern Duvalias’. It is found extensively in the tropical parts of Namibia north of Windhoek, but well east of the Namib Desert. In Botswana it is also widely distributed, mainly around the edge of the country, although it is apparently rare in the sandy part north of the Okavango Delta and in the dry south-west. There are also several records from Zimbabwe, all of them away from the wetter, central highlands. In South Africa it occurs in the Kimberley district, in the former Transvaal and sporadically in KwaZulu-Natal (though it is very common in the driest parts of the Tugela River valley) and this is the only country where it occurs well outside the tropics, since it is recorded as far south as near Douglas, along the Orange River. There are also a few records from the south of Angola, where it has been collected a few times in the vicinity of Xangongo (Roçadas). Further records exist from Malawi, where it occurs in Colophospermum mopane woodland in the relatively low-lying valley of the Shire River south of Liwonde, from Swaziland and from Zambia, where it may well be more widely distributed. It was also mentioned as growing in Mozambique and the only specimen that I have seen from there is a collection of L.C. Leach from near Goba at the foot of the Lebombo Mountains.

description: From the Rivier Zonder Einde Mountains near Genadendal (the south-western limit) through the Eastern Province, Transkei, Natal, Zululand and Swaziland to the Eastern and Northern Transvaal (Zoutpansberg). A. arborescens is the most widely distributed of all the South African Aloes, its South African range being well over 1,000 miles, excluding Southern Rhodesia, in which territory Mr. H. Basil Christian records that it also occurs in the Inyanga, Urntali and Melsetter districts, and at the Victoria Falls, Mr. Christian has also found A. arborescens on the top of Dedza Mountain in Nyasaland. In the Cape, A. arborescens occurs between the first mountain ranges and the sea, and further east and north from the Drakensberg to the sea, and along the Zoutpansberg in the Northern Transvaal. It is found from sea level (Mossel Bay, Transkei, Southern Natal) to altitudes of over 6,000 ft. (Mount Anderson, and mountain tops west of Pilgrims Rest in the Eastern Transvaal).

description: South West Africa, Bechuanaland Protectorate, Northern Transvaal, Portuguese East Africa. Cited localities include Okahandja, Rehoboth, Kuisib, Windhoek, Hoachanas, Fish River near Seeheirr, in the Auob valley (150 miles south-east of Marienthal), Ababes (fl. May), between Tsubgaus and Ganaams (fl. Dec), between Namseb and Nomtsas (fl. Dec). Plentiful between Otjiwarongo and Tsumeb. In Bechuanaland Protectorate, A. rubrolutea is recorded at Olifantskloof in the far west, to Molepolole near Gaberones. In the northern Transvaal the species is found in Mopani-veld and bush-veld north of the Zoutpansberg east and west of Wylies Poort, northwards to near Beit Bridge and Messina, fairly plentiful near Waterpoort, Soutpan and Vivo. description: Erica taylorii occurs in two widely separated areas, the Swartberg Range above Ladismith and Oudtshoorn, and the Cederberg Mountains east of Clanwilliam. It is variable in the number of leaves per whorl, number of flowers per inflorescence and in the size of the corolla, which can be hairy or glabrous. The Cederberg populations have 3- or 4-nate leaves, whereas the Swartberg populations have only 4-nate leaves. Most plants have a hairy corolla with the variation in indumentum not linked to any specific area. The totally glabrous form occurs in Schumann 380 with the type collection having a few flowers with some hairs on the corolla lobes and slightly more in Vlok 1263. The Seweweekspoort populations are all finely puberulous. All the collections from the Cederberg have a hairy corolla, except for a few branches on Bond 1403, which have very short hairs only on the corolla lobes. The eastern populations of the species are confined to the Swartberg Range in two widely separated areas, one above Ladismith along the Klein Swartberg in the region of Seweweekspoort Mtn, and the other some 90 kms to the east in the Tierberg area above Oudtshoorn.

description: In Q. arenicola, which has a more easterly distribution on the edge of the winter-rainfall region and the western margin of the Great Karoo, the ascending to spreading tubercles on the stems are arranged fairly exactly into four neat tiers, the stems are uniformly grey- to purple-green and the leaf-rudiment may be subtended by a pair of stipular denticles surrounded by a few ‘hairs’. The flowers are borne on peduncular patches at more or less any height on the stems but with a preponderance towards the base. In Q. armata, which occurs along the west coast in Namaqualand, the spreading to descending tubercles on the stem are rather untidily arranged into four or five irregular rows, the stems are brightly mottled with purple to blackish on a grey to green background and the leaf-rudiment is mainly without stipular denticles and without hairs. The flowers are borne mainly towards the apex of the stems.

description: Eastern and Northern Transvaal; Southern Rhodesia, Lydenburg District: Verraaiers Nek 16 miles north of Lydenburg, further north on slopes north-west of Ohrigstad, west of Longsight, plentiful between Burgersfort and Penge Mine. Secocoeniland: Jane Furse Hospital, near Magnet Heights, near Schoonoord and generally towards the Olifants River. In the Waterberg on rocky bushveld hills 3 miles north of Warmbaths, and along the road to Nylstroom, between Nylstroom and Naboomspruit, along foothills of the Strydpoortberg, 12 miles north-east of Potgietersrust. Pietersburg District: Between Chunies Poort and Malips Drift; slopes of the Wolkberg south-east of Boyne; abundant for a few miles east of Smits Drift along the Haenertsburg road about 25-28 miles east of Pietersburg. Zoutpansberg: Near Wylies Poort, and from Msequa's Poort westwards along the northern side of the Zoutpansberg towards Waterpoort. Southern Rhodesia: Mr. H. B. Christian records that this species is 'Fairly common in Matabeleland, extending to Mashonaland to within 60 miles south of Salisbury; the Matopos, Bembezi, Enkeldoorn and Victoria Districts; plentiful at the mouth of the Sabi River gorge'. description: The first record of the species is a painting by Francis Masson (BM), dated 1790 and annotated 'Loc. nat. in collibus aridissimis Karo prope Elephants river'. Masson would have collected the bulbs during his journey to the Roggeveld, between 26 September 1774 and 20 December 1774, via what is today known as Vanrhynsdorp. The species was rediscovered by Mr H. Hall as recently as 1981, on dolomite outcrops in the low-lying Knersvlakte, just north of Vanrhynsdorp. Currently, the species is known from less than five sites on most of the major limestone outcrops of the Knersvlakte: near the Graafwater River, north and south of the Sout River, and north and south of the Vars River, in quarter degree grids 3118BC and 3118DA.

description: Scadoxus multiflorus has a very wide distribution, covering nearly the whole of the Sudano-Zambezian Region, as defined by White. It avoids the driest parts of the region, e.g. the border areas to the Karoo-Namib Region and most of the Oriental Domain and its Sahelian Extension. It occurs in the forest-savanna mosaic in the border region between the Sudano-Zambezian Region and the Guineo-Congolian Region in Zaire, Cameroun, and W. Africa. It penetrates into the Afro-montane Region throughout Tropical Africa and, locally, deep into the Guineo-Congolian Region proper (in W. Africa, as subsp. longitubus) and the Usambara-Zululand Domain (in South Africa, as subsp. katharinae [as 'katherinae']). The occurrence of S. multiflorus on the small islands of the Chagos archipelago in the Indian Ocean is most likely the result of dispersal by man. The distribution equals that of the species, excluding the lowland rain forest area of W. Africa and the coastal shrub in South Africa.

description: Dryopteris antarctica is remarkably disjunct in its distribution, occurring on the isolated island of St Paul (37°52'S, 77°35'E) in the south Indian Ocean, and in southern Africa where it occurs in Western Cape and the south-western corner of the Eastern Cape, occurring at elevations ranging from 600 to 2130 m. Surprisingly, the species is absent from the Drakensberg range where one would expect this high elevation species to occur. To the north of South Africa it is known from the source of the Pungwe River (1980 m) in eastern Zimbabwe, and Mt Mulanje in southern Malawi. In tropical East Africa it occurs on Mt Kenya (ca. 2530 m) and the Aberdare Mountains (2920 m) in Kenya, Mt Kilimanjaro (2900 m) in Tanzania, Mt Mgahinga (3192 m) in western Uganda, and the Virunga Mountains in the Southern Kivu province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It has also been reported from Volcan Sabyinyo in the neighbouring Rwanda (Pichi Sermolli 1985). The species also occurs at 1850 m on Reunion, and at 2000 m on Massif d'Andingitra in northern Madagascar.

description: The geographical distribution of these groups indicates that only Group 1 forms an isolated geographical unit. Plants from this group are restricted to the coastal plains around Port Elizabeth, and are found at an altitude lower than 300 m above sea-level. Both Groups 3 and 4 abound west of this region along the Western Cape coast. Plants from Group 3 are normally found on the sea-facing side of the Tsitsikamma Mountains at an altitude of (0-300 m) 300-900 m above sea-level, whereas individuals from Group 4 are normally found further inland but at the same altitude. Isolated collections of plants from Group 4 have also been made in the Eastern Cape region near the towns of Somerset-East and Cradock. Group 2 has the widest distribution and is commonly found between the 32° and 34°S latitudes and the 25° and 27°E longitudes, with further extensions along the southern and eastern coasts. The Western and Eastern Cape coast therefore house a sympatric distribution of individuals from Groups 2, 3 and 4.

description: Piaranthus cornutus was the most widely distributed taxon in Piaranthus until Huerniopsis decipiens was moved to Piaranthus. It is found in southern Namibia, and from there sporadically into the western corner of the Free State. In Namibia it is found from Aus southwards (mainly in the mountains) to Rosh Pinah. East of this there are sporadic records around Klein Karas, around the foot of the Great Karas Mountains and near Warmbad. In Namaqualand it is uncommon below the escarpment, where there are only two records. Otherwise it is far more plentiful further inland, where it is found from north of Steinkopf and in the gneiss hills around Springbok along the eastern flanks of the Kamiesberg to near Kliprand. Further eastwards it is fairly common around Pofadder but becomes much rarer eastwards to Kakamas and Prieska. To the south of this, recent collecting has indicated that it is common between Calvinia and Williston as well as around Carnarvon. Further east it occurs rather more sporadically near Strydenburg and Britstown and even extends as far as the Free State near Lückhoff. Yet further south it has been seen very sporadically near Fraserburg but no other localities are known on the southern portion of the Roggeveld Plateau. This is a much more considerable range than was known to Meve, who mentioned that it ‘is a taxon of the winter-rainfall area (single exceptions known)’. In fact P. cornutus is relatively widely found in the summer-rainfall zone.

description: Piaranthus parvulus occurs in the southern portion of the Ceres Karoo, from around the foot of Skittery Kloof southwards to Matjiesfontein on the western side and on the eastern side in the area below Verlatekloof. description: Tridentea gemmiflora is of very wide occurrence in South Africa. While it is nowhere particularly common, it is probably most readily encountered in the Worcester-Robertson Karoo and the Little Karoo, where it is known from about midway between Worcester and Robertson eastwards to Oudtshoorn, Willowmore and Steytlerville. The southernmost point in its distribution is on the coastal plain south of the Langeberg between Swellendam and Heidelberg. North of the Little Karoo it is of very sporadic occurrence in the Great Karoo from Fraserburg eastwards to Graaff-Reinet and north-east to the Free State around Lückhoff, with a single record from the southern part of the former Transvaal.

description: Tromotriche revoluta occurs fairly widely on the Knersvlakte of southern Namaqualand and around its margins. It is rather more common on the eastern boundaries of the Knersvlakte on the slopes of the escarpment from north-west and south of Loeriesfontein to Vanrhyn’s Pass and then southwards along the valley of the Olifants River to near Clanwilliam. Along the escarpment it is found among rocks and bushes and can even be seen quite high up on steep slopes or on the summits above them. In these rather sheltered circumstances the stems are somewhat scattered but can be quite long (up to 300 mm tall) and relatively thick (25 mm).

According to Leach it is ‘restricted to a small area in the Soutpansberg in the vicinity of Wyllie’s Poort’ and all the specimens that he cited came from this spot. My own exploration has revealed that it is considerably more widely distributed. Material has been located from near the western corner of the Soutpansberg near Soutpan via Waterpoort to Wyllie’s Poort and eastwards at least to Nwanedi. This amounts to a total distance of at least 100 km in an east-west direction along the mountain chain.

description: Stapelia hirsuta is particularly variable in the pubescence of the stems. In Namaqualand the stems are always finely pubescent. In the south-western Cape almost glabrous stems are found on granites from Malmesbury to Paarl and on sandstone substrates in the Hottentots Holland, Hex River and Langeberg ranges of the Cape Fold mountains. As soon as the shale areas in the Little Karoo are entered, the stems become more pubescent. This is true throughout the Little Karoo, and where sandstone and shale come close to one another glabrous-stemmed plants (var. vetula) may be found growing quite close to ones with pubescent stems (var. hirsuta). East of Willowmore all forms of S. hirsuta have glabrous stems. In this region they are found mainly on sandstones but also sometimes on shale (e.g. in the former Transkei). Here the common species occurring on shales or dolerite with pubescent stems is S. grandiflora.

description: Stapelia rubiginosa is endemic to the Richtersveld on the southern side of the Orange River, in the north-westernmost corner of South Africa. It was originally collected west of the escarpment at Remhoogte and also at Cornell’s Kop in 1947. Both of these localities are at altitudes of below 350 m where extreme desertification may have led to this species dying out in the area. More recent collections all seem to have been made at higher altitudes (500 -800 m) in the hilly country north-west, north and south of Eksteenfontein.

description: Stapelia similis is widely distributed in the southern part of Namibia and in Namaqualand and Bushmanland of South Africa. In Namibia it is mainly found along the eastern margin of the Namib from south-west of Rehoboth to Witpütz. Records have also been made on many of the isolated hills and mountains in the southern part of the desert from Sturmhaube southwards to the Aurus Mountains. This entire area receives winter-rainfall. The species also occurs around the southern and western edge of the Great Karas Mountains and in the Warmbad district. In South Africa it is particularly well known from the Richtersveld but it is also recorded eastwards along the Orange River to Upington. Giess mentioned material that he had seen from the Brandberg in central Namibia but it is probable that this referred to the small- and dark-flowered plants discussed below under S. kwebensis.

description: Very few collections of S. teretifolius have been made since the time of Drège. Recent collectors have established the existance of S. teretifolius on several neighbouring peaks in the Du Toits Kloof-Wemmershoek area, yet the exact locality of Malbrokskloof where Drège made two collections of this species on different occasions is still uncertain. After studying Drège's itinerary and the other plant material collected at Malbrokskloof it seems to me most probable that Malbrokskloof is the large kloof (unnamed on modern maps), which is situated between Hugenoots Kop, the Seven Sisters and the Havekwas range, about one and a half miles north of the summit of Du Toits Kloof pass. Jf this assumption is correct, then the present known distribution range extends from just north of Du Toits Kloof southwards to Wemmershoek Peak and eastwards to Du Toits Peak.

The most westerly populations occur on Platberg in the Fern-kloof Nature Reserve, while the most easterly occur some ten kilometres further along the range in an area just beyond Rocklands Peak. Between these two points, in a narrow belt about one kilometre wide, occasional scattered populations can be found.

From there, populations are rather more sporadically dispersed, south-westwards to Bains Kloof, Du Toit's Kloof, Wemmershoek and Kaaimansgat, and south-eastwards along the Worcester mountains to Naudesberg, above Koo.

description: One of the commonest Cape proteas, P. laurifolia is widely distributed on inland mountains in the south-western Cape. From the Bokkeveld Berg escarpment near Nieuwoudtville there is an almost unbroken series of populations extending southwards along the Gifberg, Cedarberg, Olifants River, Cold Bokkeveld, Tulbagh, Bain's Kloof, Du Toit's Kloof, Paarl and Franschhoek mountains to Villiersdorp, whence it is further dispersed eastwards over the northern slopes of the Riviersonderend range to McGregor. Western outliers occur on Heerenlogementberg, Piketberg and Paardeberg (Malmesbury). Further inland, P. laurifolia skirts the western edge of the Karoo, occurring along the Cedarberg-Swartruggens escarpment, at Karoo Poort, on the Bonteberg, on the Witteberg at Matjiesfontein as well as on the Worcester-Hex River mountains and also the Langeberg at Montagu, finally appearing on the Anysberg at the western end of the Little Karoo.

Further east it is also found on Groenlandberg near Houwhoek, in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve and along the coast at Rooi Els, Betty's Bay and Kleinmond, extending to the Klein River mountains, Hermanus, where the most easterly populations are found between Vogelgat and Stanford.

description: At the time of writing, P. odorata must be numbered among the few proteas that can be regarded as rare or endangered species. Whatever its distribution area may have been in the past - and it seems likely that it has always been restricted to the Swartland - P. odorata is today confined to two small refugia within the region. The most extensive stand, consisting of several hundred individuals (perhaps as many as a thousand) is about 50 km north of Cape Town on the farm Groenfontein which is situated to the east of Katzenberg and a few kilometres south of the railway line linking Kalbaskraal and Groenrivier siding. There is also a small group between the bridge (over this railway line) on the national road to Malmesbury and Kalbaskraal village. To the east a second population consisting of barely a dozen individuals still survives at Joostenberg. The Klapmuts population discovered by Acocks now appears to have been wiped out due to extensive roadworks in the area.

description: P. restionifolia is principally dispersed along the western margin of Breede River Valley from Rawsonville, Brandvlei and Worcester, to Doom River and Scherpenheuwel in the south-east. Populations also occur at Villiersdorp, Don-kerhoek, Teewaterskloof and Ezeljacht; along the eastern foothills of the Groenlandberg and Houw Hoek ranges to Bot River and the northern foothills of Babylons Tower, Caledon. Late last century this species was also collected at Kleinvlei outspan in the Cold Bokkeveld - very isolated from the main distribution area, but although no subsequent records have been made it is quite possible that P. restionifolia still occurs there. Although it may be locally frequent, P. restionifolia seldom attracts attention and con-sequently it remains a poorly known species.

There are also populations along the crest of the Witteberg, near Matjiesfontein, this being the most easterly point of the species' range.

description: Although P. rupicola is one of the most widely distributed of the Cape proteas, it occurs only sporadically within its range. From Somerset Sneeuwkop in the Hottentots Holland mountains, it is dispersed northwards to Jonkershoek, Simonsberg, Wemmershoek, Slanghoek and Groot Winterhoek above Tulbagh, extending eastwards to Matroosberg, Keeromsberg and Dassieshoek at Robertson; thence in a more or less straight line throughout the Swartberg, Kamanassie and Kouga mountains, ultimately reaching Cockscomb Peak in the Groot Winterhoek range near Uitenhage. P. rupicola is apparently absent from the southern Cape coastal ranges, that is, the Riviersonderend, Langeberg, Outeniqua and Tzitzikama mountains.

description: In South Africa Polystichum luctuosum occurs from the Eastern Cape through KwaZulu-Natal to the northeastern parts of the Free State, Mpumalanga, and the Northern Province. It also extends to the lower elevations in the western parts of Lesotho, the higher-lying part of Swaziland, and with isolated populations occurring along the eastern escarpment in Zimbabwe. Outside of Africa the species occurs on Reunion and the central parts of Madagascar, extending to the Indian subcontinent, Pakistan, China, Vietnam, South Korea and Japan (Honsyu, Sikoku and Kyusyu).

description: Herpetineuron toccoae is widely distributed in temperate as well as tropical regions. In the New World H. toccoae is present and somewhat common in the mountains of North and South Carolina, Georgia, and Tennessee, in the Ozarkian Highlands, in scattered localities in southern Illinois, western Florida, Louisiana, eastern Texas, Mexico, Guatemala. Honduras, Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, and SE Brazil. In the Old World it occurs in the Himalayas and southern India. Sri Lanka, Manchuria and southeastern China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Celebes, Sumatra, Java, and New Caledonia. H. toccoae is present in South Africa, West Africa, and Tanzania. The species is absent in Europe and Central Asia.

description: C. ruscifolia has a very extensive distribution. It grows, as a matter of fact, within the whole area of the Cape Flora, from the Cape Peninsula to Namaqualand and Calvinia in the north and to Humansdorp in the east. The distribution of the [male]-and [female]-plants in different parts of the area is very peculiar. From the Cape Peninsula, where the species, so far as I know, has been collected not less than 29 times, not a single [male]-specimen has been found, while two collections out of three from the Paarl distr. consist of [male] [male]. In other districts the [female]-plants seem to be in the majority, but usually too little material is collected to justify any far-reaching conclusions. The occurrence of exclusively [female]-plants in the Cape Peninsula has been observed several times by different authors.

description: Hoodia alstonii has an unusual distribution within the winter-rainfall region of southern Namibia and in the western parts of the Northern Cape. It occurs in three apparently discrete areas which are separated at their nearest points by some 150 km. The northernmost of these consists of several gravelly, quartz and schist hillsides in the Namib Desert from 30-50 km east of Lüderitz northwards to Uri Hauchab. Here plants are extremely common, for example on the Hahlenberg, roughly in the centre of this area, but are much rarer on other similar prominences nearby and the species may be more widely distributed in these parts than the records show. The other two areas where it occurs are along the lower reaches of the Orange River. The more extensive of these is in the mountainous country along the lower Orange River from Umdaus north of Steinkopf to west of Sendelingsdrift. Here H. alstonii grows on both banks of the river (i.e. in Namibia and in South Africa) and is mainly found on schist slopes and outcrops but occasionally also on quartz ridges. The remaining area is in the flat-topped quartz mountains in the vicinity of Aggenys, Pella and Pofadder, where it seems to occur mainly on the summits of these ridges but in this case only on the south bank of the river i.e. in South Africa. This area falls outside the winter-rainfall region.

description: Hoodia flava is not quite as widely distributed as H. officinalis. It is recorded in southern Namibia from the eastern and southern flanks of the Great Karas Mountains. In the Northern Cape it occurs just east of the winter-rainfall region in the quartz hills around Pofadder in Bushmanland but it is much more regularly encountered on the southern edge of Bushmanland from Calvinia to Carnarvon, from where it extends southwards across the Great Karoo towards Prince Albert and Rietbron. It is quite plentiful in some localities between Calvinia, Britstown and Beaufort West, but becomes rare further south towards Prince Albert and Rietbron. It appears to be very rare between Pofadder and Vanwyksvlei, where there is a gap in the documented distribution.

description: Orbea namaquensis is of relatively restricted distribution in Namaqualand and is only known to the south of the Orange River. Below the escarpment, it is found from Doornpoort (a little south of Kubus in the Richtersveld) to near Soebatsfontein. Although I have found it within 10 km of the sea between Port Nolloth and Grootmis, it generally appears to be rare in the coastal sandveld. Above the escarpment it is fairly common in the hills from Steinkopf southwards to near the Buffels River, south of Springbok. Further east it rapidly disappears, with a single record from north-east of Concordia and one from Pella, near Pofadder. It seems to be exclusively a species of the arid part of the winter-rainfall area.

description: Stapelia flavopurpurea has a wide distribution in Namibia and South Africa. In Namibia plants have been found from Nauchas, a little south-west of Windhoek, across a broad swathe of arid territory southwards to near Witpütz and eastwards to Warmbad, i.e. generally west of the Kalahari sands and east of the Namib proper and also outside the winter-rainfall zone in the south-west. In South Africa it is found from Twee Rivieren southwards via Upington, Kenhardt and Carnarvon to near Britstown. There are two records from the eastern side of the Kamiesberg, but generally it keeps well east of the winter-rainfall region.

description: Stapelia kwebensis has the broadest distribution in an east-west direction of any species of Stapelia. In Namibia it is distributed widely and has been recorded from the northern parts of the Kaokoveld to the Great Karas Mountains in the south, generally east of the Namib and west of the Kalahari. In Botswana it is found particularly in the calcareous areas of the Mkari-kari and other pans in the centre but also occurs westwards towards the border with Namibia and eastwards towards the valley of the Limpopo River in Zimbabwe and the northernmost part of South Africa. It is found further east in Zimbabwe in the Sabi River valley and has been collected near Pafuri in Mozambique.

description: Orbea variegata is widespread in the south-western Cape, with its northernmost stations around Lambert’s Bay and Clanwilliam, where increasing aridity is evidently a limiting factor. Further eastwards it grows on the coastal plain south of the Langeberg to Riversdale, Mossel Bay, Humansdorp and near Hankey. There are also scattered records from the Karoo around Worcester and in the southern parts of the Great Karoo, e.g. Matjiesfontein, and specimens from Willowmore and Steytlerville. Some of these might well represent escapes from local gardens, in which it is frequently cultivated, rather than records of naturally occurring populations.

description: Hoodia gordonii is extremely widely distributed. It is found from the Brandberg in Namibia (about 21° S) southwards into the Northern and Western Cape, where it is of scattered occurrence over much of the Great Karoo to the Ceres Karoo in the south-west and the Prince Albert district (33°S) in the extreme south. It is found as far east as near Kimberley in the Northern Cape and near Fauresmith in the Free State. Generally H. gordonii avoids the winter-rainfall areas, only occurring towards their drier margins where some summer rainfall is received - for example it is hardly recorded at all from Namaqualand. Exceptions to this are found along the Doorn River from north of Tulpfontein to Doringbos, on the Ceres Karoo and along the northern margins of the Cedarberg. This is also the only area where it will be found occasionally growing on soils derived from sandstones. Apart from winter-rainfall, another limiting factor appears to be frost, to which H. gordonii is very susceptible. As a consequence, it is absent from many of the higher areas of the Roggeveld Plateau, for example.

description: Stapeliopsis saxatilis is the most widely distributed species in the genus and is known from somewhat north-east of Vanrhynsdorp on the southern boundary of Namaqualand to near Uitenhage. The species is found widely in the Worcester-Robertson Karoo and Little Karoo, and it grows at the southern edge of the Great Karoo from Laingsburg to east of Prince Albert along the northern slopes of the Swartberg. From Worcester to Willowmore it occurs fairly frequently. East of Willowmore it is found in a few isolated spots, mainly on the lower slopes of the sandstone mountains and as far east as Cockscomb Peak to the south of Steytlerville. There are a few isolated records from the Ceres Karoo. Considerably further to the north it has been found quite widely from Vanrhyn’s Pass in the west to south-east and north-east of Calvinia as well as up to about 50 km north of Nieuwoudtville. This part of the distribution appears to be disjunct from the remainder further south.

description: The most widely distributed and variable species in the genus, M. cucullatus is found on Table Mountain Sandstone formations in most mountain ranges in the south western and southern Cape. Isolated outliers occur in moist refugia within otherwise arid montane habitats like the Rooiberg in the Little Karoo, the Klein Swartberg, above Ladismith, and at a single locality in the Kouga Mountains (Baviaanskloof Forest Reserve); the latter site being the most isolated and also the most easterly for the species. Such a distribution pattern suggests that M. cucullatus may have been more widely distributed in the past but that increasing aridification at the northern and eastern perimeters of its range has greatly reduced its occurrence there.

description: Confined to an area of little more than five square kilometres in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve, about seventy-five kilometres south east of Cape Town. The largest population is found on the upper south east slopes of Kogelberg Peak, extending to the head of Spinnekopsneskloof. Smaller, isolated groups occur nearby at the north western end of the Dwars River mountains (also known as Groenlandberg on some maps), as well as on the south east slopes of Kudu Peak, a prominent eminence situated immediately adjacent to Kogelberg. Not only is its spatial distribution very localised, its altitudinal range is equally compressed, being limited to a zone between 1000 and 1260 m.

description: S. confusa has the widest distribution range in the genus, occuring from the Cedarberg in the north west to Mannetjiesberg in the Unionale district. The apparent absence of this species from the Langeberg and Outeniqua ranges is puzzling for there are many peaks in the coastal ranges of a suitable altitude to harbour S. confusa. This may be due to inadequate collecting but such a suggestion is hardly tenable as the Langeberg-Outeniqua area is just as well known botanically as the Swartberg. The eastward extension thus takes place entirely along the Witteberg, Swartberg and Kamanassie ranges. No other species extends as far east as S. confusa.

description: Protea acaulos is widespread through much of the southwestern Cape, from Pakhuis in the Cedarberg at its northern limits to the mountains above Bredasdorp at the most southerly point of its range. Populations occur in the Cedarberg, Olifants River, Cold Bokkeveld, Twenty Four Rivers, Tulbagh, Wolseley, Wellington, Du Toit's Kloof and Drakenstein mountains, as well as on Piketberg, at Dassenberg and at Kalabaskraal. In the south, it is common in the Hottentots Holland range, the Kogelberg Forest Reserve and Klein River mountains, as well as along the Riviersonderend range as far east as Storms Vlei.

description: P. acuminata has a curiously fragmented distribution range occurring in three areas in the western Cape, each isolated from the other. The most northerly population is on the Nieuwoudtville escarpment between the summit of Van Rhyns Pass and Meulsteenvlei. There is then a break in the distribution range until the species reappears in the Cedarberg mountains, being dispersed in a southerly direction to Elandskloof near Citrusdal and westwards into the sandveld as far as Bergvalei near Paleisheuwel. From these points there is again a sharp interruption in the distribution pattern until the most southerly populations are reached in the Stettynskloof mountains, Worcester, and at Kaaimansgat near Villiersdorp.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. amplexicaulis is fairly widespread on the central mountain ranges of the south western Cape. The most northerly populations occur in the Cold Bokkeveld near Bokkeveld Tafelberg, spreading southwards to the peaks surrounding Ceres, including Baviaansberg on the margin of the Ceres Karoo in the east, and the Witzenberg in the west. From there the species is distributed along the mountains encompassing the Breede River valley; along the eastern chain to Worcester and the Langeberg as far as Koo and along the western chain to Tulbagh, Bain's Kloof, Du Toit's Kloof and French Hoek, thence to Villiersdorp and along both north and south sides of the Riviersonderend range (including the Caledon Swartberg), reaching Riviersonderend and McGregor at its south-easterly limit.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: The major coastal mountains of the southern Cape are the natural habitat of P. aurea. ssp. aurea. Populations are found as far west as Galgeberg near Greyton on the Riviersonderend mountains, whence its range extends eastwards along the Langeberg and Outeniqua mountains as far as George.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Populations of P. burchellii range from Sir Lowry's Pass in the south along the lower slopes of the Hottentots-Holland, Helderberg, Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, Paarl and Wellington mountains, as far as Saron in the north; to the west of this line it is distributed sporadically over the coastal flats, mainly at Kraaifontein, Dassenberg and Paardeberg (Malmesbury) with a few isolated outliers between Aurora and Redelinghuys, north of Piketberg. Further inland there are extensive stands in the upper Breede River valley between Worcester and Tulbagh, as well as an isolated population at the north end of the Agter Witzenberg Vlakte.P. burchellii is now extinct in the Cape Peninsula although up until the turn of the last century, plants could still be found growing at Sea Point as well as above Cape Town on Lion's Head. In 1893 Prof. Peter MacOwan noted that it had become rare on Lion's Head but the last recorded collection from this locality was made by Dr R. Marloth, as late as 1903. Thereafter the remaining survivors were apparently rapidly exterminated.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: There are four principal occurrences of P. caespitosa in the coastal mountains of the south-western Cape, each isolated from the other and each tending to be slightly different. (1) At the extreme east of the species' range, populations are found on Olifantsberg, above Genadendal, in the Riviersonderend mountains. (2) The largest populations occur in the Hottentots Holland mountains, on Somerset Sneeuwkop, The Triplets, Victoria Peak and the Ridge Peaks above Langrivier, Jonkershoek. (3) The most northerly outliers are on the upper shale band of Wellington Sneeuwkop, while the most southerly population (4), occurs between Kogelberg Peak and Five Beacon Ridge, at the head of Spinnekopsnes-kloof.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: From Worcester, where P. canaliculata occurs on the Brandwacht, Fonteintjiesberg and Keeromsberg mountains, populations extend eastwards to Koo and thence inland to the Waboomsberg, Voetpadsberg, Witteberg, Klein Swartberg and Swartberg ranges. The area around the Swartberg Pass summit appears to be the species' most easterly limit.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Practically all the known records of P. comptonii are from the Saddleback mountains above Barberton. Here the species is most easily seen along the Barberton-Havelock road. Other collections have been made to the west of Barberton at Kaapse Hoop and also in Natal, where material has been collected from the hills around Vryheid.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: At one time P. convexa was thought to be confined to the Witteberg Range in the vicinity of Matjiesfontein and Whitehill but populations have since been found on the Elandsberg to the north of the Klein Swartberg mountains and also in the northern foothills of the Klein Swartberg near Seven Weeks Poort.

description: Populations of P. cordata are rather sporadically dispersed from Du Toit's Kloof southwards to the Hottentots Holland mountains, where it is most abundant near Grabouw, at Houw Hoek, in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve, at Kogel Bay, Kleinmond and Bot River; thence throughout the Klein River mountains to Hermanus and the mountains at Napier and Bredasdorp. Isolated populations are found along the Riviersonderend range, while the most easterly record is from Lemoenshoek Peak on the Langeberg near Grootvadersbos.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea coronata has a curiously disjunct distribution range in the south-western and southern Cape. In the west it is common on the Cape Peninsula and in the Drakenstein mountains between Du Toit's Peak, Villiersdorp and French Hoek, extending along the Hottentots Holland mountains to Stellenbosch, Somerset West, Betty's Bay, Kleinmond, Grabouw and Genadendal, reaching Sondags Kloof near Napier in the south. Then there is a gap in the range with populations reappearing in the southern foothills of the Langeberg and Outeniqua's, between Riversdale and George, where a further disjunction occurs. The most easterly populations range from Witelsbos to Humansdorp, also occurring in the Suurberg mountains in the Uitenhage district.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. cryophila occurs exclusively in the Cedarberg Wilderness area. Its range extends over approximately 25 km in a north-south direction, from Sneeuwkop in the north to Sneeuwberg in the south-west. Between these points it will be found on most of the higher Cedarberg peaks, such as Shadow Peak, along Langberg and on Tafelberg.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Recorded from a single locality only, P. curvata is one of the most narrowly endemic of all South African proteas. A solitary population is distributed along the summit ridge and southern lip of a low koppie on the farm Claremont Vale, near Caledonian siding, in the drainage basin of the Suidkaap River, a few kilometres north of Barberton, Transvaal. (Late Note: Recently Mr. Steve Fourie of the Transvaal Department of Nature Conservation has discovered further populations of P. curvata on land adjoining Claremont Vale. Thus this rare species is less vulnerable than it was previously believed to be.)
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Gifberg to Port Elizabeth.

description: This is one of the most widespread of the Cape proteas, occurring at many places throughout the south-western, southern and eastern Cape, between Slangvlei in the southern Cedarberg at its north-western limit and Beggarsbush Forest Reserve, about 20 kilometres east of Grahamstown, at the eastern extremity of its range. It will be found on all the major mountain ranges between these two points; - on Piketberg, the Olifants River, central Cold Bokkeveld, Tulbagh, Du Toits Kloof, Drakenstein, Hottentots Holland, Klein-berg River, Riviersonderend and Bredasdorp mountains with outliers on the Potberg. It is also found over most of the high ground on the Cape Peninsula. East of Tulbagh the species occurs sporadically on the Worcester mountains; thence along the Langeberg, Outeniqua, Tzitzikama, Winterhoek, Suuranys and Van Stadensberg to Grahamstown. However, P. cynaroides is absent from the dry interior ranges, notably the Hex River, Witteberg, Swartberg, Kamanassie, Kouga and Baviaanskloof mountains.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea decurrens is rather erratically distributed over much of the southern Cape coastal peneplain, as well as in the foothills of the Langeberg. From Shaw's Pass at Caledon, scattered populations are found on the north slopes of the Potberg, at Swellendam, Heidelberg, Riversdale, Albertinia and Herbertsdale, with the most easterly populations occurring along the lower north slopes of the Langeberg, between Cloete's Pass and Attaqua's Kloof.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: A strictly eastern Cape species, P. foliosa ranges from the Van Stadensberg mountains eastwards to Uitenhage, Bethelsdorp and Port Elizabeth, wherever there are out-croppings of Table Mountain Sandstone. Populations situated further east at Bushmans River Poort, Alexandria and further inland on the hills around Riebeek East and Grahamstown, occur exclusively on Witteberg Quartzite.

description: One of the most widespread Cape proteas, P. grandiceps is found on most coastal mountains between Bainskloof and Uitenhage. Its range extends from Wellington Sneeuwkop at the extreme north-west to the Slanghoek, Du Toitskloof, Jonkershoek and Hottentots Holland mountains, thence eastwards along the Riviersonderend range to Swellendam. From Swellendam it is dispersed rather more erratically along the Langeberg, Outeniqua and Tzitzikama mountains as far as Formosa Peak. Further inland the species has been reported from the Kamanassie range, while the most easterly populations occur in the Great Winterhoek mountains on the Cockscomb and Strydomsberg near Uitenhage. In the past P. grandiceps was occasionally seen on Table Mountain, where it occurred from Devil's Peak along the western slopes to Corridor Buttress in the Twelve Apostles. Described as being 'locally common on saddle between Table Mountain and Devil's Peak' in 1919 by Neville Pillans, it has since been exterminated there and at most other sites but a few plants may still survive on Spring Buttress in the Twelve Apostles where it was last seen by Miss Elsie Esterhuysen in 1942.

description: Only one naturally occurring population of P. holosericea is known, consisting of slightly fewer than 254 cmdividuals (in 1978). The plants are dispersed along the north-east ridge of Sawedge Peak at an elevation of approximately 1200 m. No other groups are known at present. Although their possible existence cannot be ruled out it is notable that P. magnifica is abundant on the adjacent peaks of Rabiesberg and Naudesberg but does not occur at all on Sawedge Peak. Although their possible existence cannot be ruled out it is notable that P. magnifica is abundant on the adjacent peaks of Rabiesberg and Naudes-berg but does not occur at all on Sawedge Peak.

description: From Goudini, Worcester and Brandvlei, P. humiflora is dispersed along the lower northern foothills of the Riviersonderend mountains between Jonas Kop and McGregor; thence to Robertson and the Waboomsberg Range northeast of Montagu. From Montagu, populations are also scattered along the northern foothills of the Langeberg as far as Lemoenshoek beyond Barrydale, with isolated occurrences on the Warmwaterberg, reaching Rooiberg, a mountain island in the Little Karoo near Calitzdorp, at the species' eastern limits.

description: Thus far P. inopina has been recorded exclusively from a relatively small area at the north-west end of the Olifants River mountains, roughly midway between the summit of Piekenierskloof Pass and the village of Paleisheuwel. Two major eminences, Bergvlei-se-Berg and Pretoriuskrans, dominate the northern section of the range. Saddled between them are the farms Mieliedraai and Pretoriuskrans whence the only records of this species come. From sightings reported by the local farmers, however, it would appear that P. inopina is probably more widely distributed in this area.

description: As construed here, P. lacticolor has a relatively limited distribution range in the higher coastal mountains of the extreme south-western Cape. Scattered populations occur from Mt. Lebanon on Groenlandberg near Houw Hoek, to the Hottentots Holland peaks, especially Somerset Sneeuwkop and The Triplets; from there into the upper Jonkershoek valley and northwards to the Du Toit's Kloof-Slanghoek mountains, with the most northerly outliers occurring on Great Wellington Sneeuwkop.

description: Populations of P. laevis are sporadically distributed throughout the higher inland mountains of the southwestern Cape. They range from Sneeuwkop in the Cedarberg, southwards throughout the Cold Bokkeveld and Swart-ruggens to Baviaansberg, the Skurfteberg and Hex River mountains; thence to Waaihoek and Fonteintjiesberg, above Worcester, with the most southerly outliers occurring at Rietvlei, in the Waboomsberg range near Montagu.

description: One of the unusual features of P. lorea is its rather fragmented distribution pattern. The most northerly records are from an outlying population at Ceres. However, the main occurrence is along the lower slopes of the Drakenstein and Hottentots Holland mountains from Wemmershoek to Franschhoek, Helderberg and Grabouw. From there populations occur sporadically along the lower south slopes of the Riviersonderend and Langeberg ranges, on the Caledon Swartberg, at Genadendal, Riviersonderend, Swellendam, Grootvadersbos and Riversdale. There are no records east of Riversdale although it is possible that P. lorea will eventually be found as far east as Herbertsdale.

description: At present P. mucronifolia is restricted to two farms, both situated to the south of Voelvlei Dam near Hermon, more or less midway between Wellington and Tulbagh. These are Kasteelskloof, owned by the Department of Forestry and the adjacent farm Elandskloof on which the privately owned Elandsberg Nature Reserve is located. Populations which previously occurred on the commonage at Gouda and at Slagter's Pad Farm can no longer be traced. One can only guess at the original distribution range, but it seems fairly clear that this species was contained within an area bounded by the Berg River in the west, the northern foothills of the Elandsberg mountains in the east, the village of Hermon to the south and the Roodezand Pass (where Niven originally discovered it) in the north.

description: Protea mundii has a curiously disjunct distribution. It occurs principally along the south-eastern Cape coastal belt between George and the Groendal Wilderness area in the Strydoms-berg range near Uitenhage. Between these points it is abundant in the Outeniqua, Tzitzikamma, Van Stadens and Great Winterhoek, as well as parts of the Baviaanskloof mountains. However, about 300 km to the west, there are several populations in the mountains between Betty's Bay and Hermanus, completely isolated from the main distribution area. These are at Platbos and Wynand Louwsbos in the Kogelberg Forest Reserve; at Fairy Glen, Kleinmond, and on Maan-skynkop in the Klein River Mountains. Despite many eminently suitable habitats on the Langeberg, there are no authentic records of P. mundii from that range.

description: This species has a rather limited distribution area which extends in a narrow belt along the mountain ranges enclosing the western side of the Upper Breede River valley, from Wemmershoek in the south to the Dutoitskloof, Kluitjieskraal, Voelvlei, Tulbagh and Witzenberg mountains reaching Michell's Pass, Ceres, at the north-easterly extremity of its range.

description: A few isolated stands on the south slopes of Klein Winterhoek, Tulbagh, constitute the most north-westerly occurrence of this species. However, from Jonkershoek, the populations are more evenly dispersed, skirting the Hottentots Holland foothills to Kogel Bay, thence eastwards to the Groenlandberg, Riviersonderend, Caledon Swartberg and Potberg to Swellendam. From there, P. neriifolia ranges along the Langeberg, Aasvoelberg (Albertinia), Outeniqua, Tzitzikama and Van Stadensberg mountains to Groot Winterhoek, Uitenhage, reaching Port Elizabeth in the extreme east. There are no authentic records as yet from the Swartberg but it does occur on the Rooiberg (Ladismith), Kamanassie and Koega mountains in the eastern Langkloof.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: This is one of the widest-ranging of the Cape proteas occurring from the Gifberg above van Rhynsdorp, in the northwest, to the Great Winterhoek and van Stadens mountains near Uitenhage in the south-east. Between these points, P. nitida is found on sandstone hillsides and mountains of the Cape Folded Belt within an area bounded by the Cedarberg, Cold Bokkeveld, Worcester, Swartberg, Kamanassie, Kouga and Baviaanskloof mountains in the interior and by the southern and south western Cape coastline.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: At present, P. nubigena is known from a single locality at 2300 m (7600 ft) in the Natal Drakensberg. This site, in the Royal Natal National Park, is a turfy, south-east facing, almost vertical cliff above Policeman's Helmet ridge, on the ridge leading up to The Witches. Naturally, it is more than likely that the species occurs at other localities on the walls of the Amphitheatre, or even further south towards Giant's Castle, but the preferred habitat is so inaccessible that only teams of climbers using ropes will be able to investigate similar sites where this species might be expected to occur. We will therefore have to await the results of some fairly intrepid botanical exploration before the further range of P. nubigena becomes known.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea pendula is distributed over a comparatively small area of the central south-western Cape, from Tafelberg in the south-eastern Cedarberg, throughout the Skurweberg, Swartruggens and eastern Cold Bokkeveld mountains, to Gydo and Baviaansberg, near Ceres.

description: The most northerly recorded occurrence of P. piscina is on Grootberg in the Cedarberg, whence its range extends southwards through the southern Cedarberg and Cold Bokkeveld, following the line of the Olifants River Valley, to the Witsenberg and Gydo Pass. Isolated populations also grow on the Piketberg. At Swellendam, further populations occur along the southern foothills of the Langeberg, extending eastwards as far as Plattekloof, between Heidelberg and Riversdale.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: P. pityphylla has a very restricted distribution range, extending over a mere 50 kilometres, along the semi-circle of mountains that form the southern boundary of the Ceres valley. At present, populations are known to occur between the Ceres municipal reservoir in the eastern foothills of the Skur-weberg, Slab Peak and the mountains around Michells Pass and thence along the north slopes of the Hex River range to Shale Peak, Milner Peak and finally to the Outer Sanddrift Peaks, at the species' extreme easterly limits.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Until quite recently, P. pruinosa was thought to be restricted to a very short stretch of the Klein Swartberg, between Towerkop and Hoekoe, in the vicinity of Ladismith. Sightings have subsequently been reported from more easterly localities on the Swartberg Range with a definite record from a peak near Blesberg, a few kilometres east of Meiring's Poort. Thus Towerkop and Blesberg are presently the most westerly and easterly limits of the species' range, while further records from the central Swartberg can be expected in the future.
bibliographicCitation: Rourke, JP. 1980. The proteas of southern Africa. Purnell, Cape Town. [All rights reserved]

description: Protea pudens only occurs in the southern Cape, between Bredasdorp and Elim where it is restricted to a narrow strip of land approximately 10 kilometres long by 3 kilometres wide, on level flats situated to the north-west of the Heuning-rug hills on the farms Mierkraal, Rooiwal, Heuningrug and Valsvlei, at a mean elevation above sea-level of approximately 35 metres.

description: Populations of P. punctata are found on almost all the drier inland mountain ranges of the south-western and southeastern Cape, between Sneeuwkop in the central Cedarberg and Smutsberg in the Kouga mountains. Common in the Cedarberg, Cold Bokkeveld, Hex River and Worcester mountains, as well as on the Witteberg, Swartberg and Kamanassie ranges, there are even outliers on the summits of peaks fringing the Great Karoo, such as on Aasvoelberg at Willowmore. On the moister coastal ranges, a few scattered populations occur in the Tulbagh mountains, on Bailey's Peak, Wellington, at Wemmershoek and along the summit of the Riviersonderend mountains between Olifantsberg and Jonaskop.

description: Long since exterminated through agricultural development at Eerste River - formerly the most western point of its range - P. scabra is presently dispersed from Sir Lowry's Pass throughout the Grabouw Valley and Kogelberg Forest Reserve, to Hangklip, Betty's Bay, Kleinmond and Houwhoek; it is further distributed along the Klein River mountains to Hermanus and Stanford as well as the adjacent inland peaks of Babylon's Tower, Shaw's Mountain and Steen-boksberg. The northern perimeter of the species' range encompasses the Nuweberg Forest Reserve, Franschhoek Pass, Villiersdorp and the entire Riviersonderend range, both on the north and south slopes as far as McGregor and Riviersonderend respectively. There are also populations on the Caledon Swartberg.

description: Very limited in its distribution, this montane species is found mainly on the higher peaks encircling the Ceres Valley-Matroosberg, Skurfteberg, Hansiesberg, Gydoberg and Baviaansberg, but does extend northwards through the eastern Cold Bokkeveld and Swartruggens to Bokkeveld Tafelberg, reaching Blaauwkop at the northern extremity of its range.
