description: A very widely distributed species found mainly on the interior (rather than the extreme coastal) mountains of the southwestern and southern Cape. P. scolopendriifolia ranges from the Middelberg area of the central Cedarberg, southwards through the Cold Bokkeveld to the Ceres, Tulbagh, Wellington, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Somerset West and Villiersdorp mountains, extending eastwards along the Riviersonderend and Langeberg ranges as far as Grootvadersbos. From the Worcester/Montagu area, populations are distributed even further eastwards, to the Witteberg and thence along the Swartberg and Kammanassie ranges eventually reaching Hoopsberg at the western end of the Kouga mountains.

description: This species has a moderately wide distribution range along the coastal flats and forelands of the south-western Cape. Scattered stands occur from Nardouw (a little north of Clanwilliam), southwards throughout the sandveld to Paleisheuwel, Hopefield, Malmesbury, Darling, Riebeek Kasteel, Bellville and Eerste River. On the Cape Peninsula, it still survives near Hout Bay, Kommetjie and in the Cape Point Nature Reserve, but has been exterminated on the Cape Flats between Salt River and Retreat, where it was abundant in the past. Isolated populations on the shores of the Bot River lagoon and between Hawston and Sandbaai, near Hermanus, constitute the most southerly occurrence of P. scolymocephala.

description: One of the most widespread South African proteas, P. simplex is distributed across the eastern part of the country from Keiskamma Hoek and an area along the coast just west of East London, through the Eastern Cape, Transkei and Natal to the highlands of Swaziland, with outlying populations reaching the Wolkberg area of the Drakensberg in the northern Transvaal.

description: This species is widely dispersed in the coastal mountains of the south-western and southern Cape, from Cape Town to Riversdale. description: Protea subulifolia is distributed over most of the southern part of the south-western Cape. From Villiersdorp and the Elgin valley it is dispersed southwards to Bot River, Hawston, Stanford and Elim, with the most southerly populations occurring at Mierkraal near Bredasdorp and at Springfontein near Cape Agulhas.

description: P. sulphurea has a curiously disjunct distribution. A few rather scattered populations occur in the Hex River mountains and on Sawedge Peak, near Worcester. Further inland it becomes more abundant, particularly on the mountainous Waboomberg range near Koo and Montagu, as well as on the koppies around Touws River, Laingsburg and the Witteberg at Matjiesfontein, from where occasional populations are distributed along the northern foothills of the Swartberg to as far east as Prince Albert. In Namaqualand there is also a stand of P. sulphurea but completely isolated from the more southerly distribution area described above, with the majority of plants being restricted to the higher peaks of the Kamiesberg, particularly Rooiberg, also known as Welcome Kop.

description: Polystichum transvaalense is widely distributed in temperate and tropical Africa. The distribution largely follows the escarpment and mountain ranges on the eastern parts of the continent. In South Africa it occurs from the Drakensberg foothills in the Eastern Cape along the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg escarpment, the Eastern Cape and southern KwaZulu-Natal midlands, the Free State-KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga-Northern Province escarpments to the Soutpansberg in the Northern Province. A single collection is also known from the foothills of the Riviersonderend Mountains in the southern Cape. In Zimbabwe it is found in the Chimanimani and Vumba Mountains extending to the Zomba Plateau, the Kirk Mountains and the Nyika Plateau in Malawi and Zambia. In Tanzania it occupies the Uluguru- and Usambara Mountains, Mt. Meru and Mt. Kilimanjaro. Further north it occurs in the mountainous areas of Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, the Imatong Mountains in Sudan and the Kivu Ridge in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A disjunction in this pattern arise in that P. transvaalense is also found on Mt. Cameroon and Bioko in the Gulf of Guinea.

description: Polystichum wilsonii has a wide distribution ranging from Africa to the Uttar Pradesh mountains in northern India, and to Bhutan, China (Szechuan) and Taiwan (Ilan, Taichung, Hsinchu). In the study area P. wilsonii has a disjunct distribution. In South Africa it occurs on the southern Cape mountains, along the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg and into Lesotho, extending along the Free State-KwaZulu-Natal escarpment as far north as the Vryheid District. To the north it occurs in the mountainous areas of Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia and the Kivu Ridge in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The species is also known from Mt. Cameroon and the island of Bioko, 32 km from the mainland in the Gulf of Guinea. It has furthermore been recorded from Grande Comore c. 300 km from the mainland in the Mozambique channel. Although the higher ground of the Zambezian Region, which includes Zimbabwe and Malawi, supports Afromontane plant communities, it is rare in this region with only one collection known from Zimbabwe.

description: Distributed widely through Eurasia and North Africa, North America, Australia, Tasmania, and southern (but not tropical) Africa, where it is recorded so far only from Lesotho and South Africa, and reportedly also Botswana but not Namibia. In South Africa the species is scattered through the southern and eastern interior of the county along the Vaal/Orange Rivers and tributaries, and along the southern escarpment from Calvinia to Queenstown, with a few coastal stations in the southwestern and southern Cape around Velddrif, Cape Town, Bredasdorp and Uitenhage.

description: The type material of M. laxa came from Windhoek near Klaver (Van Rhynsdorp div.,) and the plant appears still to be common thereabouts, probably always on the mountain slopes above c. 180 m. Thence south and east to the southern end of the Cold Bokkeveld Mountains and the mountains around Tulbagh, Ceres, Worcester, Robertson, Montagu and Genadendal and east to the environs of Laingsburg, Ladismith, the Langeberge, and the southern flank of the Outeniqua Mountains. There is one collection from Swellendam at only 60 m above sea level: the others are all above c. 180 m and reach c. 1370 m in the Cold Bokkeveld Mountains and Klein Swartberg. The typical plant is more or less leafy up to the inflorescences; many of the plants from higher altitudes have the leaves crowded near the base of stem, possibly in response to harsher conditions: for example, on the flanks of the Klein Swartberg at 1300 m (Moffett & Steensma 3841, E, PRE, STE) in 'sandy rocky talus below lowest rock band' the plants have scanty radical leaves and long nude scarcely branched stems, while on 'dunes of Breede River' at 60 m, the lowest elevation recorded, the plants are richly branched and leafy (Acocks 22246, PRE).
bibliographicCitation: Hilliard, OM. 1994. The Manuleae: a tribe of Scrophulariaceae. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh. [All rights reserved]

description: Dicranella hookeri is a pan-south-temperate species. It is widely distributed in southern South America and extends along the Andean chain from Chile, through Bolivia, Peru and Ecuador to Colombia and Venezuela in the northern Andes where it occurs at high elevations of 3800-4100 m. It also occurs in south-eastern Australia and Tasmania and New Zealand as D. jamesonii (Mitt.) Broth.). Additionally, D. hookeri is known from Tristan da Cunha and Gough Island and penetrates into the Subantarctic and to some volcanic islands in the northern maritime Antarctic, including the South Sandwich Islands and Deception Island in the South Shetland Islands archipelago. In South Africa Dicranella hookeri occurs on the Highveld of the eastern Free State and Mpumalanga.

description: The geographical range of Racomitrium lamprocarpum is somewhat anomalous but it can be otherwise designated as bipolar. The species has the main centre of its distribution in the Southern Hemisphere where it has a pan- Holantarctic temperate range. It has maximum occurrence in southern South America at the western fringes of the continent, ranging from lat. ca 39°S in the Valdivian province to the Cape Horn area and the Falkland Islands with isolated stations in the Juan Fernandez Islands, and along the Andean chain in Bolivia, Peru, Colombia and Venezuela. It recurs in the Cape area of South Africa and on some islands in the Southern Ocean, including Gough Island in the South Atlantic, Marion Island in the Prince Edward Islands archipelago, Iles Kerguelen and Heard Island in the Kerguelen Province of the Subantarctic and on Macquarie Island in the Australasian sector of Subantarctica. In the Northern Hemisphere R. lamprocarpum has a narrow geographical range on the Iberian Peninsula.

It is found along the eastern flank of the escarpment, from Hellskloof to Eksteenfontein and further east to Pofadder in Bushmanland and Warmbad in south-eastern Namibia. It is extremely uncommon in the area between Pofadder and Warmbad, where it appears to be known from only two collections, one of which is the sole known record from Namibia. From the Steinkopf area, where it is more common, it continues southwards, again always on the eastern and much drier side of the Kamiesberg and reaches its southernmost limits to the north-east of Kamieskroon.

description: Piaranthus decipiens occurs over a very wide area in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa, around the northern and eastern edges of the driest parts of the Kalahari. In Namibia it is found in the central area from Nauchas eastwards to Epukiro and Gobabis and southwards towards Leonardville. It is widely and rather scantily recorded in Botswana. The area in Botswana around Ghanzi is particularly poorly collected and it is undoubtedly more plentiful than the two recent collections which have been made there indicate. It is rather better known in the south-east, where it is found from Lephephe southwards to Lobatse. It has been most frequently collected in South Africa from about 50 km south of Prieska northwards to the edge of the Kalahari and eastwards past Vryburg to Mafikeng and to around Schweizer-Reinecke.

description: Orbea melanantha has a rather more restricted distribution than its close relative O. lutea. It has been recorded in Mozambique from near sea level around Maputo to 300 m above sea level near Moamba, with a single record from further north near Vilankulo, also close to the coast. It is mainly known at relatively high altitudes of between 1000 and 1700 m in the northern part of South Africa where it is found from the Soutpansberg southwards and westwards to near Pretoria and towards the edge of the escarpment near Tzaneen and around Groblersdal. It is often locally very common and although it occurs near to where O. lutea has been recorded, the two species have never been observed growing sympatrically.

It is widely distributed in South West Africa, from the Warmbad district in the south to Klein Karas, Kanus, Inachab and elsewhere to Usakos in the north. There appears to be no record of its northern limit.

From Swartberg Pass there are collections both of ssp. apiculata and ssp. calycina. It is apparent, however, that the former subspecies grows on higher altitudes and the latter on the lower slopes of the mountain. Ssp. lanceolata occurs on stony or clayey, sometimes calcareous soil on flats and lower hills.

Plants of subsp. guttata are often of very scattered occurrence and invariably grow on stony slopes under bushes. In the eastern part of the distribution they are often associated with sandstone mountains and, for example in the Suurberg and in the Longkloof, they grow on north-facing slopes in semi-arid spots with shallow soils overlaying rock slabs surrounded by fynbos elements. In such spots they often cohabit with various species of Crassula and Haworthia.

description: Subsp. zebrina is widely and very patchily distributed across southern Africa. On the eastern side of the subcontinent it is quite common in Limpopo Province, mainly in the somewhat lower-lying basin of the Limpopo River. In Zimbabwe it is found in the south only, also mainly along the valley of the Limpopo. Records have also been made in Swaziland, southern Mozambique and in KwaZulu-Natal as far south as Eshowe. Towards the west the distribution becomes far more disjointed and it occurs in an area around Serowe in Botswana and in two widely separated areas in Namibia. One of these is around the base of the Great Karas Mountains in the south and the other is near the foot of the Waterberg in the north.

description: Var. cornutus occurs over much of the range of the species. Here the corolla is 15-30 mm in diameter. It is rarely flat and the corolla lobes generally rise somewhat from their bases and then spread towards their tips. The lobes have an ovate base and taper from this gradually to a slender tip. Along the eastern flank of the Kamiesberg, the flowers have a creamy background and are especially boldly marked with maroon spots which become transversely elongated towards the bases of the lobes. Further east and north, the colour becomes more variable. The background is cream to white but the spots vary from bold as before to very fine and, in some cases, are even entirely absent.

description: Var. grandiflora is probably the best recorded of all southern African stapeliads apart, perhaps, from Hoodia gordonii. It is widely, if rather scantily distributed over the Great Karoo from Kenhardt and Carnarvon southwards to around Fraserburg and then east to Graaff-Reinet and into the Free State. There are some records from the Little Karoo from Calitzdorp eastwards to around Willowmore and it is not uncommon in the Steytlerville, Port Elizabeth and Grahamstown areas.
